main.title: Learn to program — your first programs, from Scratch to C
main.why: the Main track starts by looking inside the computer, and the first builds ask you to write small C programs. This step teaches you to program at all, so those builds are reachable on day one. No experience assumed.

mustKnow.t: What a program is: a precise list of instructions a computer follows, with no guessing
The building blocks every language shares
c: Values and variables
Conditions (if / else) and boolean expressions
Loops (while, for)
Functions: naming a piece of work, inputs (parameters) and outputs (return values)

mustKnow.t: Thinking in steps: breaking a problem into smaller problems (decomposition) and writing pseudocode first
Your first compiled language, C: source code, the compiler (clang or gcc), running the program from a terminal
Types in C: int, char, float, bool, strings as arrays of char; why the computer needs to know a value's size
Arrays: many values of the same type side by side in memory; indexing from 0
Bugs are normal: reading a compiler error top to bottom, printf debugging, and using a debugger to step through a line at a time

niche: Integer overflow and floating-point imprecision (you'll see why in Week 1)
Command-line arguments: argc and argv
Why C has no bounds checking and what a buffer overflow is
Style: naming, indentation and comments that say why, not what

resources.text: CS50x (Harvard, free): lectures 0 (Scratch), 1 (C) and 2 (Arrays) — lectures, sections and problem sets, done in the CS50 browser IDE (cs50.dev) so there is nothing to install
CS50x shorts and notes for each week (if a lecture moves too fast)
Exercism C track (free) for extra practice with automatic checks

sessions.label: Lecture 0 + Scratch
sessions.text: Watch the CS50x lecture 0. Build the Problem Set 0 Scratch project: a small game or story that uses at least one loop, one condition and one variable.

sessions.label: Lecture 1: C
sessions.text: Watch the CS50x lecture 1 and read its notes. Write hello.c in cs50.dev, compile it with make, run it, then break it on purpose and read the compiler error.

sessions.label: Problem Set 1
sessions.text: Solve Problem Set 1 (Mario and Cash, or the more comfortable versions). Write pseudocode before each program. Run check50 until every check is green.

sessions.label: Lecture 2: arrays
sessions.text: Watch the CS50x lecture 2: compiling in four steps, debugging with debug50, arrays, strings and command-line arguments.

sessions.label: Problem Set 2
sessions.text: Solve Problem Set 2 (Scrabble and Readability, then Caesar or Substitution). Step through one bug with debug50 instead of guessing.

main.doneWhen: you can write, compile and debug a C program with loops, functions and arrays from a blank file, and explain what each line does.

main.title: How a computer works
main.why: every abstraction you use (JS, Docker, Kubernetes) is eventually a CPU executing instructions on bytes in memory.

mustKnow.t: Information as bits
c: Binary, decimal, hexadecimal; converting between them by hand
Bits, bytes, words; KB vs KiB
Signed integers and two's complement; overflow
Floating point (IEEE 754) and why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3
Text encoding: ASCII, Unicode, code points, UTF-8 vs UTF-16

mustKnow.t: Logic and hardware
c: Logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, XOR) and how they build an adder
The CPU: registers, ALU, control unit, clock speed
The fetch-decode-execute cycle
Instruction sets (x86, ARM) and machine code vs assembly

mustKnow.t: Memory
c: Memory hierarchy: registers → L1/L2/L3 cache → RAM → SSD/disk → network
Approximate latencies at each level ("latency numbers every programmer should know")
Addresses and pointers; what "a value lives at an address" means

mustKnow.t: From source code to running program
c: Compiler, interpreter, JIT compiler; what each does
Source → assembly → object file → linker → executable

niche: Endianness (big vs little endian) and why network protocols care
Cache lines (64 bytes) and why iterating an array row-by-row is faster than column-by- column
Branch prediction and why sorted data can make loops faster
Unicode normalization and grapheme clusters (why emoji "length" is weird in JS)
Integer overflow bugs in real systems (Ariane 5, Y2038)

resources.text: Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software (Charles Petzold, 2nd ed.) — read chapters on number systems, logic gates, adders, memory and the CPU; skim the rest
Crash Course Computer Science (YouTube), episodes 1-10
"Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know" (search it; many versions)

checklist.text: Petzold, number systems + binary chapters. Convert 10 numbers between binary/decimal/hex by hand.
Petzold, logic gates + adders. Draw a half adder and full adder on paper.
Petzold, memory + CPU chapters, or Crash Course CS episodes 5-9.
Write a tiny C program, compile it with gcc -S, and read the generated assembly. Write your first note: "What happens when I run a program".

main.doneWhen: you can explain, with a drawing, how a CPU runs one instruction, and why reading from RAM is ~100x slower than from L1 cache.

main.title: Operating systems I — processes, threads, memory
main.why: every program you run, from your browser tabs to a web server or a Docker container, is a process. You need to know what that means.

mustKnow.t: What an OS is: the kernel, user mode vs kernel mode
Processes
c: A process = program + memory + state; the PCB (process control block)
Process states (running, ready, blocked)
fork(), exec(), wait(); parent and child processes; PIDs
Context switching and its cost

mustKnow.t: CPU scheduling: time slices, round robin, priorities, why your app "pauses"
Memory
c: Virtual memory and address spaces; why each process thinks it owns all memory
Pages, page tables, the TLB, page faults
A process's memory layout: code, data, heap, stack
Stack vs heap: what goes where, stack overflow, memory leaks

mustKnow.t: Threads
c: Threads vs processes: what's shared and what isn't
Concurrency vs parallelism

niche: Copy-on-write after fork() (why forking is cheap)
Zombie and orphan processes
Swap and thrashing; the Linux OOM killer (why your container gets "OOMKilled")
Memory-mapped files (mmap)
Green threads / user-space threads vs OS threads (relevant to Go, Java virtual threads)

resources.text: OSTEP: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (free) — chapters 4-6 (processes, process API, limited direct execution), 7 (scheduling intro), 13-16 and 18 (address spaces, memory API, address translation, segmentation, paging intro), 26 (concurrency intro)
Julia Evans' zines on Linux and processes (wizardzines.com)

checklist.text: OSTEP ch. 4-5. Run ps aux and top; find the PID of your browser.
OSTEP ch. 6-7. Write down what a context switch saves and restores.
OSTEP ch. 13-16, 18. Draw a process's memory layout from memory.
In C: write a program that fork() s, prints both PIDs, and wait() s. Then a program that recurses until stack overflow. Then read OSTEP ch. 26.

main.doneWhen: you can explain what a process is, why two processes can't read each other's memory, and the difference between a process and a thread.

main.title: Operating systems II — files, syscalls, I/O, concurrency
main.why: every file read, network request and log line in your app is a system call. Concurrency bugs are the hardest bugs you'll face.

mustKnow.t: System calls: the boundary between your code and the kernel; strace
Files and file systems
c: Everything-is-a-file; file descriptors (0, 1, 2 = stdin, stdout, stderr)
open, read, write, close; inodes, directories, hard vs soft links
Buffering: why write doesn't always hit the disk; fsync

mustKnow.t: I/O models
c: Blocking vs non-blocking I/O
I/O multiplexing: select, poll, epoll (the foundation of Node.js and NGINX)

mustKnow.t: Concurrency
c: Race conditions and critical sections
Locks/mutexes, condition variables, semaphores
Deadlock: the four conditions and how to avoid it

mustKnow.t: Inter-process communication: pipes, signals, sockets, shared memory

niche: epoll vs kqueue vs io_uring (how modern servers do async I/O)
File descriptor limits (ulimit -n) and "too many open files" in production
Atomic operations and compare-and-swap (CAS)
The thundering herd problem
Signals: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL vs SIGINT (why graceful shutdown matters in Kubernetes)

resources.text: OSTEP chapters 28-32 (locks, condition variables, semaphores, concurrency bugs), 33 (event-based concurrency — read twice, it's Node.js), 39-40 (files and directories, file system implementation)
Julia Evans' strace zine

checklist.text: OSTEP ch. 39. Run strace cat somefile and identify every syscall.
OSTEP ch. 28-30. Write down a race condition example in your own words.
OSTEP ch. 31-33. Note how event-based concurrency differs from threads.
In Java, C or Python: two threads incrementing a shared counter 1M times without a lock (see the wrong result), then with a lock. Then strace a Node.js script that reads a file.

main.doneWhen: you can explain what a file descriptor is, why a race condition happens, and how one thread can handle thousands of connections with epoll.

main.title: Linux and the shell
main.why: every server you deploy to is Linux. Being slow in the terminal makes every later topic slower.

mustKnow.t: The filesystem layout: /, /etc, /var, /usr, /home, /tmp, /proc, /dev
Navigation and files: ls, cd, cp, mv, rm, find, cat, less, head, tail -f
Permissions: users, groups, rwx, octal (755, 644), chmod, chown, sudo, root
Shell fundamentals
c: The shell is a program; bash vs zsh
Environment variables, PATH, export,.bashrc
Pipes and redirection: |, >, >>, 2>&1
Exit codes, &&, ||

mustKnow.t: Text processing: grep, sed, awk, sort, uniq, wc, cut, xargs, jq
Processes from the shell: ps, top / htop, kill, jobs, &, nohup
Networking from the shell: curl, ping, ss / netstat, lsof -i, dig, ssh, scp
Package managers (apt), services (systemctl), logs (journalctl)
Shell scripting basics: variables, conditionals, loops, functions, shebang

niche: /proc as a live window into the kernel (/proc/<pid>/status, /proc/cpuinfo)
SSH keys, ~/.ssh/config, agent forwarding, port forwarding/tunnels
tmux for sessions that survive disconnects
Cron syntax (you'll see it again in Kubernetes CronJobs)
set -euo pipefail in scripts and why it prevents silent failures

resources.text: MIT Missing Semester — lectures 1, 2, 4 and 5 (shell, scripting, data wrangling, command-line environment); lecture 3 on Vim is optional
The Linux Command Line by William Shotts (free PDF at linuxcommand.org)
OverTheWire Bandit — a game that teaches Linux by doing

checklist.text: Missing Semester lecture 1-2 + exercises. If on Windows, install WSL2 Ubuntu first.
Missing Semester lecture 4 (data wrangling). Use grep / awk / sort on a real log file.
Missing Semester lecture 5. Explore /proc for a running process.
OverTheWire Bandit levels 0-15. Write a backup script with timestamps and set - euo pipefail.

main.doneWhen: you can find which process is using port 3000, kill it, and write a script that greps errors out of a log and counts them, without searching the web.

main.title: Git, from the inside
main.why: you use Git daily. Once you see it's just a small database of snapshots, merge conflicts and rebases stop being scary.

mustKnow.t: The object model
c: Blobs (file contents), trees (directories), commits (snapshot + parent + message), tags
Content addressing: every object is named by the hash of its content
The.git folder: objects/, refs/, HEAD, index

mustKnow.t: Refs: a branch is a file containing a commit hash; HEAD points to a branch; detached HEAD
The three areas: working directory, index (staging area), repository
Operations, explained by what they do to the graph
c: commit, branch, checkout / switch, merge (fast-forward vs three-way), rebase, cherry-pick, reset (soft/mixed/hard), revert, stash
Remotes: fetch vs pull, push, tracking branches, origin/main

mustKnow.t: Undoing mistakes safely with reflog
Team workflows: feature branches, pull requests, trunk-based development, conventional commits

niche: Packfiles and delta compression (why.git stays small)
git bisect to find which commit introduced a bug
git blame -w -C and git log -S (pickaxe search)
Interactive rebase (rebase -i) for clean history; --fixup and --autosquash
Signed commits;.gitattributes; Git hooks (pre-commit)
SHA-1 to SHA-256 transition

resources.text: Pro Git book (free) — chapters 2, 3 and 10 (Git Internals)
Learn Git Branching — interactive visual exercises
Mary Rose Cook's essay Git from the inside out

checklist.text: Pro Git ch. 10.1-10.3 (objects, refs). Open.git/ in a repo and find a commit object.
Learn Git Branching, the "Main" levels.
Pro Git ch. 3 (branching). Practice merge vs rebase on a toy repo and draw the graph each time.
Create a commit by hand with git hash-object -w, git update-index, git write-tree, git commit-tree, git update-ref. Then use git bisect on a toy repo with a planted bug.

main.doneWhen: you can explain what a branch physically is on disk, and what rebase does to commit hashes and why.

main.title: Networking — IP, TCP, UDP, DNS
main.why: every API call, every database query and every Kubernetes service is network traffic. Most production mysteries are network mysteries.

mustKnow.t: Layered models: OSI (7 layers) vs TCP/IP (4 layers); encapsulation
Link layer: MAC addresses, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP, switches
Network layer (IP)
c: IPv4 addresses, IPv6 basics
Subnets and CIDR notation (10.0.0.0/16), private IP ranges
Routers, routing tables, default gateway, TTL, traceroute
NAT and why your laptop's IP isn't your public IP

mustKnow.t: Transport layer
c: Ports and sockets (IP + port + protocol)
TCP: three-way handshake, sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmission, flow control (window), congestion control (slow start), four-way close, TIME_WAIT
UDP: when it's better than TCP (DNS, video, games, QUIC)

mustKnow.t: DNS
c: The hierarchy: root → TLD → authoritative servers; recursive resolvers
Record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SRV
TTLs and caching at every level

mustKnow.t: DHCP: how your device gets an IP
Sockets API: socket, bind, listen, accept, connect

niche: Head-of-line blocking in TCP (and why HTTP/3 moved to UDP)
Nagle's algorithm and TCP_NODELAY
MTU, fragmentation and path MTU discovery
Ephemeral port exhaustion under high load
0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1 binding (why your Docker container "isn't reachable")
Anycast (how CDNs and 8.8.8.8 work)
BGP at a high level: how the internet's networks find each other

resources.text: High Performance Browser Networking by Ilya Grigorik (free) — chapters 1-3 (latency, TCP, UDP)
Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (Kurose & Ross) — chapters 1, 3 and 4 as reference; Kurose's own lecture videos are free on YouTube
Julia Evans' Networking! ACK! zine and her post on how DNS works
Beej's Guide to Network Programming (free)

checklist.text: Kurose ch. 1 (or videos). Run ip addr, ip route, traceroute google.com; explain each line.
HPBN ch. 1-2. Draw the TCP handshake and slow start.
DNS: Julia Evans' post + dig +trace example.com. Write down every server queried.

Build a TCP echo server and client in Java (ServerSocket and Socket, from your Java track), or with Node's net module if you already know JavaScript. Capture the traffic in Wireshark; find SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK and FIN.

main.doneWhen: you can explain everything that happens between pressing Enter and the first byte of a TCP connection being sent, including DNS.

main.title: HTTP and TLS
main.why: HTTP is the language of everything you build. You'll write a server that speaks it with no framework.

mustKnow.t: HTTP/1.1 message anatomy: request line, headers, blank line, body; status line
Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS; safe vs idempotent
Headers: Host, Content-Type, Content-Length, Accept, Authorization, User- Agent, Location
Cookies: Set-Cookie, attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Domain, Path, Max-Age)
Caching: Cache-Control (max-age, no-cache vs no-store, public/private, immutable), ETag / If-None-Match, Last-Modified, Vary
Connection management: keep-alive, chunked transfer encoding, compression (gzip, brotli)
HTTP/2 (binary framing, multiplexing, header compression) and HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP)
CORS: same-origin policy, simple vs preflight requests, Access-Control-Allow-* headers
TLS
c: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, hashing, digital signatures
The TLS 1.3 handshake; certificates, chains of trust, certificate authorities
What HTTPS protects (content, integrity) and what it doesn't (the domain via SNI, timing)

niche: 502 vs 503 vs 504: which component is failing (you'll see these from NGINX)
Vary header and cache poisoning
HSTS and preload lists
Certificate pinning, OCSP stapling, Let's Encrypt and the ACME protocol
HTTP request smuggling (why proxies must agree on Content-Length)
TLS session resumption and 0-RTT
Range requests (how video seeking and resumable downloads work)

resources.text: MDN HTTP guide — Overview, Messages, Caching, Cookies, CORS, Redirections
HPBN chapters 4 (TLS), 9-12 (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2)
The Illustrated TLS 1.3 Connection — every byte of a handshake explained
CodeCrafters "Build your own HTTP server" (optional guided version)
HTTP/3 explained (Daniel Stenberg, free): HPBN predates HTTP/3 and QUIC

checklist.text: MDN Overview + Messages. Use curl -v on 5 sites and read every header.
MDN Caching + Cookies + CORS. Explain no-cache vs no-store in your notes.
HPBN ch. 4 + Illustrated TLS 1.3. Open a site's certificate in your browser and trace its chain.

Build an HTTP/1.1 server on raw TCP (Java ServerSocket or Node net; no HTTP library): parse requests, serve static files with correct Content-Type, 404s, keep-alive, and an ETag - based 304. Test with curl -v and a browser.

main.doneWhen: your server serves a real HTML page to a browser, and you can explain the full journey: DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP request → response.

main.title: How the browser renders a page
main.why: HTML, CSS and JS only make sense once you know the machine that runs them.

mustKnow.t: Browser architecture: browser process, renderer processes, GPU process, network service; site isolation
Navigation: URL parsing, the network request, response, commit, and the renderer taking over
The critical rendering path
c: Bytes → characters → tokens → nodes → DOM
CSS → CSSOM; why CSS is render-blocking
Render tree (DOM + CSSOM, minus hidden nodes)
Layout (reflow): computing geometry
Paint: filling pixels into layers
Compositing: layers combined on the GPU

mustKnow.t: How scripts affect parsing: blocking <script>, async, defer, type="module"; the preload scanner
The main thread: why one long JS task freezes everything
Using DevTools: Elements, Network (waterfall), Performance (flame chart), Lighthouse

niche: Layout thrashing (forced synchronous layout) from reading offsetHeight after writes
What creates a compositor layer (transform, opacity, will-change) and the cost of too many layers
The back/forward cache (bfcache)
Resource hints: preload, prefetch, preconnect, dns-prefetch, fetchpriority
requestAnimationFrame and the 16.6 ms frame budget

resources.text: Inside look at modern web browser (Mariko Kosaka, 4 parts)
How browsers work (Tali Garsiel, on web.dev) — long; read the parsing and render tree sections
Critical rendering path on MDN

checklist.text: Inside look, parts 1-2.
Inside look, parts 3-4. Draw the pipeline DOM → CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite.
How browsers work (parsing + render tree sections).
Serve a page from your Week 7 server. Record a Performance trace in DevTools and label every phase. Add a blocking script, then defer it, and compare the traces.

main.doneWhen: you can explain why a <script> in the <head> without defer slows the page, and what happens between HTML arriving and pixels appearing.

main.title: HTML and accessibility
main.why: HTML is the structure everything else hangs on, and most developers have never learned it properly.

mustKnow.t: Document structure: doctype, <html>, <head> (meta charset, viewport, title, link, script), <body>
Semantic elements: header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer, headings hierarchy
Text, lists, links (absolute vs relative URLs), images (alt, srcset, sizes, loading="lazy"), picture, video/audio
Tables done right (thead, th scope, caption)
Forms in depth: form action / method, input types, label, name, fieldset, built-in validation, how a form submits without JS (URL-encoded vs multipart)
Block vs inline elements
Accessibility: the accessibility tree, semantic HTML first, ARIA roles/states (and the first rule of ARIA: don't use it if HTML can do it), keyboard navigation, focus management, color contrast
SEO basics: title, meta description, Open Graph, canonical URLs, structured data

niche: <button> vs <div onclick> and why it matters for keyboards and screen readers
<dialog>, <details> / <summary>, popover attribute: native components with no JS
inert attribute and focus traps
HTML parsing error recovery (why broken HTML still renders)
Character references and the XSS danger of injecting HTML
<template> and Web Components / Shadow DOM basics

resources.text: web.dev Learn HTML
web.dev Learn Accessibility
MDN HTML reference for each element as needed

checklist.text: Learn HTML modules 1-8.
Learn HTML modules on forms and images.
Learn Accessibility, first half. Turn on your OS screen reader and use a website for 10 minutes.
Build a 3-page site (home, article, contact form) in pure semantic HTML. Make the form submit to your Week 7 server and parse the URL-encoded body. Run a Lighthouse accessibility audit; reach 100.

main.doneWhen: a form on your page submits to your own server with no JavaScript, and the page is fully usable with only a keyboard.

main.title: CSS I — the cascade, box model, flow and stacking
main.why: CSS feels random only when you don't know its rules. It has very few, and they're strict.

mustKnow.t: How CSS is applied: selectors, the cascade (origin, importance, specificity, order), inheritance, initial/inherit/unset
Specificity calculation by hand
Computed values and the DevTools Computed panel
The box model: content, padding, border, margin; box-sizing
Margin collapsing
Normal flow: block and inline formatting contexts; display values
Units: px, em, rem, %, vw / vh, ch; absolute vs relative
Positioning: static, relative, absolute (containing block!), fixed, sticky
Stacking contexts and z-index: what creates a stacking context
Overflow, floats (legacy, but you'll meet them)
Colors, typography, line-height, web fonts and font-display

niche: Block formatting contexts (BFC) and why display: flow-root fixes weird layouts
Cascade layers (@layer) for managing specificity in big codebases
Logical properties (margin-inline-start) for right-to-left languages
CSS custom properties (variables) are inherited and live at runtime, unlike Sass variables
:is(),:where() (zero specificity) and:has() (the "parent selector")

resources.text: web.dev Learn CSS — modules 1-12 this week
Josh Comeau's blog posts on the box model, stacking contexts and positioning (his CSS for JavaScript Developers course is excellent if budget allows)
Specificity calculator

checklist.text: Learn CSS: box model, selectors, cascade, specificity. Calculate specificity of 10 selectors by hand.
Learn CSS: inheritance, color, sizing units, layout intro.
Positioning and z-index; Josh Comeau's stacking context post.
Style your Week 9 site with no frameworks. Then deliberately create a z-index bug and fix it by reasoning about stacking contexts.

main.doneWhen: you can predict which CSS rule wins for any element, and explain why a z- index: 9999 element can still be behind another.

main.title: CSS II — Flexbox, Grid, responsive, performance
main.why: modern layout is Flexbox and Grid. With them plus Week 10's rules, you can build any layout.

mustKnow.t: Flexbox: main/cross axis, flex-grow / shrink / basis, wrapping, alignment, gap, ordering
Grid: tracks, fr, repeat, minmax, auto-fit vs auto-fill, named areas, implicit vs explicit grid, alignment
When to use Flexbox vs Grid
Responsive design: mobile-first, media queries, fluid typography with clamp(), responsive images
Container queries
Transitions and animations; which properties are cheap to animate (transform, opacity) and why (Week 8's compositing)
Design systems basics: spacing scales, tokens
How Tailwind and CSS-in-JS work underneath (they generate ordinary CSS)

niche: min-width: 0 on flex items (the fix for overflowing flex children)
Subgrid
prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-color-scheme
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) caused by images without dimensions and late-loading fonts
content-visibility: auto for rendering performance
How CSS-in-JS can cost runtime performance compared with static CSS

resources.text: web.dev Learn CSS — Flexbox, Grid, and the remaining modules
Flexbox Froggy and Grid Garden games
Josh Comeau's An Interactive Guide to Flexbox and An Interactive Guide to CSS Grid

checklist.text: Flexbox Froggy (all levels) + Josh Comeau's Flexbox guide.
Grid Garden + Josh Comeau's Grid guide.
Learn CSS: responsive, media queries, container queries, animations.
Clone 2 real landing pages (pick ones you like) pixel-close with only HTML and CSS, fully responsive.

main.doneWhen: you can build any common layout (navbar, card grid, sidebar + content, holy grail) from a blank file without looking anything up.

main.title: JavaScript, the language I
main.why: frameworks come and go; the language underneath them stays. By now your Java track has taught you programming basics, so JS will feel familiar.

mustKnow.t: Values and types: the 7 primitives + objects; typeof quirks (null)
Primitives vs references: copying, comparing, mutating; pass-by-value-of-reference
Type coercion: == vs ===, truthy/falsy, the abstract equality algorithm at a high level
Variables: var vs let vs const; block vs function scope; the temporal dead zone
Hoisting: what is really hoisted and why
Functions: declarations vs expressions vs arrows; first-class functions; higher-order functions; default and rest parameters
Scope chain and lexical scope
Closures: what they capture, the classic loop bug, uses (private state, memoization, factories)
Objects: literals, property descriptors, getters/setters, spread, destructuring, optional chaining, nullish coalescing
Arrays: map / filter / reduce / find / some / every / flatMap, mutating vs non- mutating methods
Strings and template literals; Number precision; BigInt

niche: Object.is vs === (NaN, -0)
Property enumeration order rules
Object.freeze is shallow; structuredClone for deep copies
Tagged template literals (how styled-components and graphql tags work)
Labels and break label (rare but real)
Strict mode and what it changes

resources.text: javascript.info Part 1, sections 1-6
You Don't Know JS Yet (free on GitHub): Get Started and Scope & Closures
JavaScript: The Definitive Guide (David Flanagan, 7th ed.) as reference

checklist.text: javascript.info sections 2 (fundamentals) and 4 (objects basics).
YDKJSY Scope & Closures ch. 1-4.
YDKJSY Scope & Closures ch. 5-7 + javascript.info section 6 (advanced functions).
Implement from scratch: debounce, throttle, once, memoize, curry, deepClone, deepEqual. Write tests with Node's built-in test runner (node:test, run with node --test).

main.doneWhen: you can explain a closure with a memory diagram and predict the output of the classic for (var i...) setTimeout puzzle, and fix it two ways. Your utilities have node:test tests that pass.

main.title: JavaScript, the language II + the runtime
main.why: this, prototypes and the event loop are where most JS confusion lives. After this week, async code will stop surprising you.

mustKnow.t: this: the four binding rules (default, implicit, explicit, new), arrow functions' lexical this; call, apply, bind
Prototypes: [[Prototype]], __proto__ vs.prototype, the prototype chain, Object.create
Classes as syntax over prototypes; extends, super, private #fields, static members
Compare with your Java track: JS has prototype-based inheritance, Java has class- based
Iterators, iterables, generators, for...of; Symbol.iterator
Error handling: try/catch/finally, custom errors, error propagation in async code Modules: ESM (import / export, static, live bindings) vs CommonJS (require, dynamic, copied values)
The runtime
c: Call stack, heap, Web APIs, task (macrotask) queue, microtask queue
The event loop algorithm: run a task → drain all microtasks → maybe render → next task
Callbacks → Promises → async/await (and that await is Promise sugar)
Promise states, chaining, Promise.all / allSettled / race / any

mustKnow.t: V8 at a high level: parser → Ignition bytecode → TurboFan optimized machine code; deoptimization; hidden classes and inline caches; garbage collection (generational, mark-and-sweep)

niche: Microtask starvation (an infinite chain of Promises freezes the page)
queueMicrotask vs setTimeout(0) vs requestAnimationFrame ordering
Unhandled promise rejections and how Node treats them
Memory leaks in JS: forgotten listeners, closures holding large objects, detached DOM nodes; WeakMap / WeakRef
Async iterators and for await...of
Proxy and Reflect (how Vue's reactivity works)

resources.text: javascript.info Part 1 sections 8-11 (prototypes, classes, error handling, promises/async) and section 12-13 (generators, modules)
YDKJSY Objects & Classes
Philip Roberts' talk What the heck is the event loop anyway? and Jake Archibald's In The Loop (both YouTube)
The V8 blog: posts on Ignition/TurboFan and hidden classes ("fast properties")

sessions.text: Read the Scrum Guide and the Kanban Guide. Write a half page on what each is for and when you'd use which.

sessions.label: Break down real work
sessions.text: Take the capstone idea you're considering and break it into an epic, stories and tasks on a GitHub Projects board. Estimate each as S/M/L with a reason.

sessions.label: Write like an engineer
sessions.text: Rewrite the descriptions of three of your past PRs and one README section using Google's CL description guide. Write a one-page design doc for a small feature.

sessions.label: Run a retro
sessions.text: Run a retrospective on your own last month of the plan: what went well, what didn't, one change. Keep it in your notes.

main.doneWhen: you can break a feature into shippable tickets, write a PR description and a short design doc that a teammate can act on, and explain how your team would handle an incident.

main.title: Python as a second language
main.why: Python is the second most used language after JavaScript and the main language of AI, data and automation. You already know two languages, so this is about learning what is different, quickly, and using it for real work.

mustKnow.t: Python's model: dynamically typed, interpreted (CPython bytecode), everything is an object, indentation as syntax
Core types: int (unbounded), float, str, list, tuple, dict, set; comprehensions; slicing
Functions: default and keyword arguments, *args / **kwargs, closures, decorators
Classes, dataclasses, duck typing, dunder methods; protocols instead of interfaces
Iterators, generators and yield; context managers (with)
Modules and packages; virtual environments; dependency management with uv and pyproject.toml
Type hints and checking them (mypy or pyright); why hints don't change runtime
Python for real work: scripting files and HTTP calls, a small FastAPI service, pytest, and just enough pandas to analyse a CSV
The GIL and concurrency options (threads, asyncio, multiprocessing), compared with Node and Java

niche: Mutable default arguments
is vs ==, and small-integer caching
Free-threaded Python (PEP 703) removing the GIL
Packaging history: pip, venv, poetry, uv

resources.text: The official Python Tutorial (docs.python.org), sections 3-9
FastAPI docs: Tutorial - User Guide (first steps through dependencies and testing)
uv docs: Getting started and Working on projects
Fluent Python (Luciano Ramalho, 2nd ed.) as the deep reference
Exercism Python track (free) for practice

sessions.label: The language
sessions.text: Python Tutorial sections 3-6. Solve five Exercism Python exercises, writing each the Pythonic way (comprehensions, unpacking).

sessions.label: Classes, generators, tooling
sessions.text: Tutorial sections 7-9 plus dataclasses. Set up a uv project with pyproject.toml, ruff and pytest, with type hints checked by pyright.

sessions.label: Automate something
sessions.text: Write a script that does a chore of yours: rename files, call an API and save JSON, or parse logs from your Phase 4 API and print the slowest endpoints.

sessions.label: A FastAPI service
sessions.text: Build a small FastAPI service with typed models, a Postgres or SQLite table, dependency injection and pytest tests. Load a CSV with pandas and serve one aggregate from it.

main.doneWhen: you can write idiomatic, typed, tested Python with a proper project setup, and explain how Python differs from JavaScript and Java in typing, concurrency and packaging.

main.title: Engineering with AI coding tools
main.why: almost every engineer now writes code with AI assistants and agents. They make you faster only if you can direct them and catch their mistakes. The skill employers want is using AI and verifying it, not either one alone.

mustKnow.t: What a coding model is and isn't: predicting likely code from context; why it can be confidently wrong
Tool types: inline completion, chat in the editor, and agents that read files, run commands and edit code
Giving context: the right files, conventions (project instructions files), the goal and the constraints
Working in small, reviewable steps: plan first, one change at a time, run the tests after each
Verifying generated code: read every line, run it, test edge cases, check for invented APIs and packages
Security: never paste secrets; sandboxing agents (containers, limited permissions), prompt injection through files and web pages, supply-chain risk of suggested packages
When not to use AI: learning something for the first time, security-critical code you can't review, code you can't explain
Using AI to learn faster: asking for explanations, test cases and code review, then checking them against docs

niche: Hallucinated package names and typosquatting ('slopsquatting')
Licence and attribution questions for generated code
Measuring whether a tool actually makes you faster
Team rules: disclosure in PRs, review standards for AI-written changes

resources.text: The documentation of the AI coding tool you use (for example Claude Code, GitHub Copilot or Cursor): its best-practices and security pages
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications (free) — the prompt injection and supply chain entries
Simon Willison's blog posts on prompt injection and using LLMs for code (free)

sessions.label: Set up and learn the tool
sessions.text: Install one AI coding tool, read its best-practices and security pages, and write a project instructions file for your foundations repo (conventions, test command, what not to touch).

sessions.label: Build with it, carefully
sessions.text: Add a feature to your Phase 4 API with an agent: plan first, approve each step, run tests after each change. Keep a log of every mistake it made and how you caught it.

sessions.label: Review its work like a stranger's
sessions.text: Ask the tool for a non-trivial function (for example a retry helper with jitter). Review it line by line, write tests that break it, then fix it yourself.

sessions.label: Break it on purpose
sessions.text: Read the OWASP LLM prompt injection entry. Put a hidden instruction in a README and see whether your agent follows it. Write down the guardrails you'll keep (sandbox, permissions, no secrets).

main.doneWhen: you can ship a change made with an AI agent that you fully understand and have tested, and you can name the mistakes these tools make and how you catch each one.

main.title: Building with LLMs I — model APIs, tools and agents
main.why: products now include features built on large language models: summaries, search, support bots, agents that take actions. Building them well is backend engineering with a new, unpredictable component, so everything you know about APIs, failures and cost applies.

mustKnow.t: What an LLM does: tokens, next-token prediction, context windows, temperature; why outputs vary
Calling a model API: messages and roles, system prompts, streaming responses (SSE, Week 21), token counts and pricing
Prompting as specification: clear instructions, examples, output format; keeping prompts in version control
Structured output: asking for JSON that matches a schema and validating it (Zod or Pydantic) before trusting it
Tool calling: the model asks your code to run a function, you run it and return the result; the agent loop
Agents: when a loop of model + tools is worth it, and when a fixed pipeline is better; step limits and human approval for risky actions
The Model Context Protocol (MCP): a standard way to expose tools and data to models; writing a small MCP server
Production concerns: timeouts, retries, rate limits, fallbacks, caching, cost and latency budgets

niche: Prompt caching to cut cost and latency
Model choice: large vs small models for different steps
Batch APIs for offline work
Why frameworks (LangChain and others) change fast, and why the primitives matter more

resources.text: The developer documentation of one model provider (for example Anthropic's Claude docs or OpenAI's API docs): quickstart, messages, streaming, tool use and structured output
Model Context Protocol docs (modelcontextprotocol.io): introduction and building a server
Anthropic's article Building effective agents (free)

sessions.label: First calls
sessions.text: Read the provider's quickstart. From your Phase 4 API (TypeScript) or a Python script, make a call, stream a response, and log tokens and cost per request.

sessions.label: Structured output
sessions.text: Add an endpoint that turns free text (for example a bug report) into a validated JSON object. Reject and retry on invalid output; count how often it happens.

sessions.label: Tools and an agent loop
sessions.text: Give the model two tools backed by your API (search notes, create note). Write the agent loop yourself with a step limit and an approval step before any write.

sessions.label: An MCP server
sessions.text: Expose the same two tools as an MCP server and use it from an MCP-capable client. Write down what MCP standardises and what it doesn't.

main.doneWhen: you can add an LLM feature to an API that validates the model's output, calls tools safely, and stays inside a cost and latency budget you can state.

main.title: Building with LLMs II — retrieval, evals and guardrails
main.why: a model only knows what it was trained on and what you put in the prompt. Retrieval lets it answer from your own data, and evals tell you whether a change made it better or worse. Without evals, an AI feature is a demo, not a product.

mustKnow.t: Embeddings: turning text into vectors so similar meaning is close together; cosine similarity
Vector search: exact vs approximate nearest neighbour (HNSW), and pgvector in the Postgres you already run
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): chunk, embed, store, retrieve, put in the prompt, cite sources
Chunking and hybrid search (keywords + vectors); reranking
Evals: a test suite for model behaviour; golden datasets, graded checks, model-graded checks and their limits; running evals in CI
Guardrails: prompt injection through retrieved content, output filtering, least-privilege tools, PII handling
Observability for LLM features: logging prompts and responses safely, tracing each step, tracking cost per user

niche: Embedding model changes force re-indexing
Long context vs retrieval: when to just put everything in the prompt
Fine-tuning vs retrieval vs better prompts
Evaluating agents (task success, steps, cost) vs single answers

resources.text: pgvector README (github.com/pgvector/pgvector): installation, querying and indexing
Promptfoo docs: getting started and configuration (free, open source)
Your model provider's docs on embeddings, retrieval and building evals
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency

sessions.label: Embeddings and pgvector
sessions.text: Add pgvector to your Postgres. Embed your API's notes (or a set of docs you choose) and run similarity queries; compare exact search with an HNSW index on 10k+ rows.

sessions.label: RAG endpoint
sessions.text: Build an /ask endpoint: retrieve the top chunks, answer only from them, and return citations. Make it say 'I don't know' when nothing relevant is found.

sessions.label: Evals
sessions.text: Write 25+ eval cases in Promptfoo (good answers, refusals, injection attempts in retrieved text). Run them in CI and make one change that measurably improves the score.

sessions.label: Guardrails and tracing
sessions.text: Add a hidden instruction to one stored note and make sure your endpoint ignores it. Trace each step (retrieve, generate) with OpenTelemetry or logs, with cost per request.

main.doneWhen: your RAG endpoint answers with citations, refuses when it should, survives a prompt injection test, and has an eval suite in CI that tells you if a change made it worse.

main.title: Modules, bundlers and chunks
main.why: this answers "what are chunks and how are they served" before you touch Next.js. Every framework build is a bundler underneath.

mustKnow.t: History: script tags and globals → IIFEs → CommonJS → AMD → ES modules; why bundlers appeared
What a bundler does, step by step
c: Entry points → parse each file to an AST → find imports → build the module dependency graph (a graph traversal, DSA track week 25)
Resolve paths (node_modules, exports field, aliases)
Transform with loaders/plugins: TypeScript/JSX via Babel/SWC/esbuild, CSS, images
Wrap modules in functions, add a small runtime, emit bundles

mustKnow.t: Optimizations: minification, tree shaking (needs ESM's static structure; sideEffects flag), scope hoisting, dead code elimination
Code splitting and chunks
c: Split points: entry points, dynamic import(), shared vendor code (splitChunks)
Each split produces a chunk: a separate JS file with an id
The runtime keeps a manifest of chunk ids → URLs and loads a chunk on demand by injecting a <script> (or import()), then registers its modules
Content hashes in filenames (app.3f9a1c.js) so they can be cached forever with Cache-Control: immutable

mustKnow.t: Source maps
Dev servers and Hot Module Replacement (HMR)
Tools compared: webpack, Rollup, esbuild, Vite (native ESM in dev + Rollup/Rolldown in prod), Turbopack, Rspack; why Rust/Go tools are faster
Transpilers: Babel, SWC; polyfills vs transpiling; browserslist targets

niche: Barrel files (index.ts re-exports) killing tree shaking and slowing builds
Duplicate dependencies in a bundle (two versions of the same library)
Module Federation / micro-frontends
import.meta, top-level await and their bundling implications
Chunk loading errors after a deploy (old HTML asking for deleted chunks) and how to handle them
Monorepos and build caching (Turborepo, Nx)

resources.text: Vite docs: Why Vite, Features and Building for Production + Ronen Amiel's talk Build Your Own Webpack and his minipack repo
webpack docs: Concepts and Code Splitting (the classic model every bundler borrows)
AST Explorer to see what parsing produces

checklist.text: Vite docs: Why Vite + Features; skim webpack Concepts for the vocabulary. Paste code into AST Explorer and inspect an import node.
Watch Build Your Own Webpack and read minipack.
Code Splitting guide + Why Vite. Build a tiny Vite project with a dynamic import() and look at the output files and the Network tab.

Write your own mini bundler (~200 lines): parse with @babel/parser, build the graph, transpile, wrap modules, emit one bundle. Stretch goal: support import() by emitting a second chunk + a tiny loader.

main.doneWhen: you can explain what a chunk is, why splitting helps, and exactly how the browser fetches a chunk it didn't have.

main.title: React internals I — elements, reconciliation, Fiber
main.why: most developers use React every day without knowing what it does. This week you'll see what actually happens when you call setState.

mustKnow.t: The problem React solves: keeping UI in sync with state without manual DOM updates (your Week 14 todo app pain)
JSX compiles to function calls (jsx() / React.createElement) that return plain objects (elements)
Elements vs components vs instances vs fibers
Rendering is calling your component function; React compares the result with the previous one
Reconciliation: the diffing heuristics (different type → replace subtree; same type → update props; lists → key)
Why key matters, and why index keys break state
Fiber architecture: a fiber per element, linked as a tree (child/sibling/return), work units, interruptible rendering
Render phase (pure, can be paused/discarded) vs commit phase (DOM mutations, synchronous)
react-dom as a renderer; React Native uses the same reconciler with a different renderer

niche: Double buffering: the current tree and the work-in-progress tree
Lanes (priority model)
Why React StrictMode renders twice in development
Component identity and position: why the same component in a different place loses state
Bailouts: when React skips re-rendering a subtree

resources.text: Rodrigo Pombo's Build your own React
react.dev: Describing the UI, Render and Commit, Preserving and Resetting State
Andrew Clark's React Fiber Architecture notes (GitHub acdlite/react-fiber-architecture)
Dan Abramov's overreacted.io, especially React as a UI Runtime

checklist.text: react.dev: Describing the UI + Render and Commit + Preserving and Resetting State.
React as a UI Runtime + the Fiber architecture notes.
Build your own React, steps 0-4. Type every line yourself.
Finish Build your own React (fibers, reconciliation, function components, useState). Rebuild your Week 14 todo app on your own React.

main.doneWhen: you can explain, step by step, what happens after setState is called, up to the DOM changing.

main.title: React internals II — hooks, effects, concurrency, state
main.why: most React bugs are effect bugs and state-design bugs. This week fixes how you write React.

mustKnow.t: Hooks as an ordered list stored on the fiber (why the Rules of Hooks exist)
State: updates are queued and batched; state as a snapshot per render; updater functions
useEffect: when it runs (after paint), cleanup, the dependency array, stale closures (Week 12!)
useLayoutEffect vs useEffect; useRef; useMemo / useCallback and when they're pointless
You Might Not Need an Effect: deriving state, event handlers vs effects
Context: how it propagates, and why it re-renders all consumers
Concurrent features: useTransition, useDeferredValue, Suspense for loading states
State management: lifting state, reducers, when external stores (Zustand, Redux) help; server state vs client state (TanStack Query)
Forms: controlled vs uncontrolled
React Compiler: what automatic memoization changes

niche: useSyncExternalStore and tearing
Race conditions in data-fetching effects and how to cancel them
Error boundaries (still class-based)
Portals and event bubbling through the React tree, not the DOM tree
Profiling renders with React DevTools Profiler

resources.text: react.dev: Adding Interactivity, Managing State, Escape Hatches (all of it, especially You Might Not Need an Effect and Lifecycle of Reactive Effects)
Dan Abramov's A Complete Guide to useEffect (overreacted.io)
TkDodo's blog on React Query and state

checklist.text: react.dev Adding Interactivity + Managing State.
react.dev Escape Hatches (all pages).
A Complete Guide to useEffect. Add useEffect to your mini React from last week.
Build a React front end (Vite) for your Phase 4 API: auth, lists with pagination, forms, optimistic updates with TanStack Query. Profile it with React DevTools and remove one unnecessary re-render.

main.doneWhen: you can explain why hooks can't be inside conditions, and refactor an effect- heavy component into one with no unnecessary effects.

main.title: Next.js — rendering, hydration, Server Components and caching
main.why: you now know bundlers, React and HTTP, so Next.js becomes a combination of things you understand. The durable ideas are rendering strategies, hydration and Server Components; the framework's own caching details change every major release, so they get less time.

mustKnow.t: The problem: a plain React SPA ships an almost empty HTML page plus a large JS bundle → slow first paint, poor SEO, a blank screen on slow phones
Rendering strategies: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming SSR; tradeoffs of each
SSR mechanics: renderToString vs renderToPipeableStream; streaming HTML over chunked transfer (Week 7)
Hydration: HTML arrives and is shown → JS chunks download → React rebuilds the tree in memory and attaches event listeners to existing DOM; hydration mismatches and their causes
Next.js App Router: file-system routing, layouts, nested routes, loading.js / error.js, dynamic segments
React Server Components
c: Server components run only on the server and are never shipped as JS
The RSC payload: a serialized description of the rendered tree, with references to client components and their props
"use client" boundaries and how client components are bundled into chunks
Navigation fetches the RSC payload for the next route and merges it without a full reload

mustKnow.t: Data fetching on the server; Server Actions for mutations
Caching in Next.js 16 at the level of ideas: Cache Components and "use cache", revalidation by time and by tag
Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS; measuring in the field vs the lab
End-to-end browser tests with Playwright: testing what a user does, not how the code is built

niche: Selective/progressive hydration with Suspense boundaries
Islands architecture (Astro) as an alternative to full hydration
suppressHydrationWarning and why dates/random values cause mismatches
next build output: the .next/ folder, route and shared chunks, build manifests
<Link> prefetching of route payloads and chunks
Serialization rules at the server/client boundary (functions and classes can't cross)
server-only package to keep secrets out of client bundles
Middleware, edge vs Node runtimes and their API limits
Deployment models: Node server, standalone output, static export, serverless
Next.js Pages Router (legacy), since many codebases still use it

resources.text: Next.js docs: Getting Started (routing, layouts, server and client components, fetching data, caching)
patterns.dev rendering patterns section (free)
Josh Comeau's Making Sense of React Server Components
react.dev: renderToPipeableStream and hydrateRoot reference pages
Playwright docs: Getting started, Writing tests, Locators
@next/bundle-analyzer; web.dev's Core Web Vitals articles

sessions.label: Rendering strategies
sessions.text: patterns.dev rendering patterns: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming, islands.

sessions.label: SSR and hydration by hand
sessions.text: Express server calls renderToString and sends HTML; a client bundle (from your Vite or your own bundler) calls hydrateRoot. Cause a hydration mismatch on purpose.

sessions.label: App Router and Server Components
sessions.text: Next.js docs: routing, layouts, server and client components. Josh Comeau's RSC article.

sessions.label: Rebuild your front end
sessions.text: Rebuild your Week 24 front end in the Next.js App Router, fetching from your API on the server. Keep client components to the interactive pieces only.

sessions.label: How this page loads
sessions.text: In DevTools Network, record a first load, a <Link> navigation (find the RSC payload request and read it) and a prefetch. Write How this page loads explaining every request. Measure Core Web Vitals and improve one.

sessions.label: Playwright
sessions.text: Write Playwright tests for the three main user journeys of your app and run them in CI.

main.doneWhen: you can explain the page lifecycle from request to interactive (what ran on the server, which chunks downloaded, what the RSC payload contains), choose a rendering strategy per page, and your main journeys are covered by Playwright tests.

main.title: Design kata 2 — a news site that loads fast everywhere
main.why: the second kata uses what you just learned about bundles, React and rendering. The question is no longer only 'where is the data' but 'what does the user's phone download, and when'.

mustKnow.t: Choosing a rendering strategy per page: static, revalidated, server-rendered per request, streamed
Cache layers end to end: browser, CDN, framework cache, API cache, database
Invalidation when an article changes: tags, purges, versioned assets
Performance budgets: JS size, LCP and INP targets on a slow phone
Personalised parts on a cached page: islands of dynamic content

niche: Breaking news: a traffic spike 50x normal on one URL
Paywalls and caching per user
Images: formats, sizes, responsive loading

resources.text: Your notes from Weeks 22-25
web.dev: Core Web Vitals articles and the rendering patterns on patterns.dev, after you finish

sessions.label: Design it
sessions.text: Design a news site (home page, article pages, a personalised 'for you' rail, 50M page views a day, breaking-news spikes) in 90 minutes. Decide rendering and caching per page and the invalidation path when an editor fixes a typo.

sessions.label: Compare and revise
sessions.text: Compare with a public engineering write-up of a large news or content site's front end. Write down three differences and which you'd adopt.

sessions.label: Prove one decision
sessions.text: In your Next.js app, build one article page your way and measure LCP and JS bytes on a throttled mobile profile. Show the effect of one caching or rendering change.

main.doneWhen: you can choose a rendering and caching strategy per page and prove one choice with real measurements on a slow device.

main.title: The edge stack — proxies, load balancers, CDN, gateway and WAF
main.why: between a user and your code sit several specialised reverse proxies: a CDN, a WAF, load balancers and an API gateway. They appear in almost every production diagram, and each is a config file you can read once you know what problem it solves.

mustKnow.t: Forward proxy vs reverse proxy; why reverse proxies exist (TLS termination, static files, buffering slow clients, load balancing, hiding internals)
NGINX architecture: master + worker processes, event-driven with epoll (Week 3), why it handles huge concurrency with little memory
NGINX configuration: http / server / location blocks, location matching order, proxy_pass, upstream, X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto, gzip, proxy_cache, limit_req, TLS
Load balancing
c: L4 (TCP) vs L7 (HTTP) load balancers
Algorithms: round robin, weighted, least connections, IP hash, consistent hashing
Health checks (active vs passive), connection draining
Sticky sessions and why stateless apps avoid them

mustKnow.t: CDN
c: Edge locations (PoPs), anycast (Week 6), origin servers, origin shield
Cache keys, Cache-Control / s-maxage / stale-while-revalidate (Week 7), purging and versioned URLs
Edge compute (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge)

mustKnow.t: API gateway: one front door for many services (routing, JWT validation, rate limits and quotas, transformation); API management adds a developer portal, keys and analytics
WAF: L7 inspection with the OWASP Core Rule Set; detection vs blocking; false positives and tuning; DDoS at L3/L4 vs L7
How the layers stack in practice (DNS → CDN → WAF → LB → gateway → service), and which ones a small company actually needs

niche: proxy_buffering and why streaming/SSE responses hang behind NGINX by default
Upstream keepalive connections and their huge performance effect
Timeouts chain: client → NGINX → app → DB must be ordered sensibly
502 (upstream refused/crashed) vs 504 (upstream too slow) debugging
Client IP trust: spoofed X-Forwarded-For
Caching authenticated responses at a CDN by mistake (data leaks)
WAF bypass techniques and why a WAF is not a substitute for secure code
Other proxies: HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy, Traefik
Backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern
DNS in production: TTL strategy for migrations, geo and health-checked DNS

resources.text: NGINX Beginner's Guide and the ngx_http_proxy_module / ngx_http_upstream_module docs
Cloudflare Learning Center: reverse proxy, load balancing, CDN, WAF, DDoS, API gateway
Load Balancing interactive essay by Sam Rose (samwho.dev)
OWASP Core Rule Set documentation + Coraza (OWASP's maintained WAF engine; ModSecurity has reached end of life)
Kong Gateway getting-started docs

sessions.label: Proxies and load balancing
sessions.text: Cloudflare reverse proxy and load balancing articles + Sam Rose's load balancing essay.

sessions.label: NGINX in front of your API
sessions.text: NGINX Beginner's Guide. Put NGINX in front of 3 copies of your API: upstream, health, TLS (mkcert), gzip, static caching, limit_req.

sessions.label: Your own reverse proxy
sessions.text: Write your own reverse proxy in Node (~100 lines): round robin across 3 backends, forward headers, add X-Forwarded-For, mark a backend down after failures. Then trigger a 502 and a 504 deliberately in NGINX.

sessions.label: CDN, gateway and WAF
sessions.text: Cloudflare CDN, API gateway, WAF and DDoS articles. Check cf-cache-status / age / x-cache headers on 5 real sites with curl -I.

sessions.label: Gateway and WAF hands-on
sessions.text: Run Kong as a gateway in front of two services with JWT validation and rate limits. Put Coraza with the OWASP Core Rule Set in front of your API and fire SQL injection attempts at it; watch it block them, then find one false positive.

main.doneWhen: you can read any NGINX config and explain what happens to a request, and draw the full edge stack (DNS → CDN → WAF → LB → gateway → service) saying what each layer does and what breaks without it.

main.title: Containers and Docker
main.why: a container is just a Linux process (Week 2) with isolation. Once you see that, Docker and Kubernetes become much smaller topics.

mustKnow.t: The problem: "works on my machine", dependency conflicts, heavy VMs
What a container really is
c: A normal process isolated with namespaces (PID, mount, network, UTS, IPC, user)
Resource-limited with cgroups (CPU, memory)
A root filesystem from a layered image (OverlayFS) via chroot / pivot_root

mustKnow.t: Containers vs VMs (shared kernel vs hypervisor)
Images: layers, layer caching, registries, tags vs digests, the OCI standard
Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD vs ENTRYPOINT, ENV, ARG, EXPOSE, WORKDIR, USER,.dockerignore; instruction order for cache efficiency
Multi-stage builds; small base images (alpine, slim, distroless)
Container runtime stack: Docker CLI → dockerd → containerd → runc
Networking: bridge network, port publishing, container DNS; volumes and bind mounts
Docker Compose for multi-container local environments

niche: PID 1 problem: signals and zombie reaping (tini, --init); why your app ignores SIGTERM in a container
Running as root inside containers and the security risk
Memory limits vs what Node/Java think is available
Image vulnerability scanning (Trivy) and SBOMs
Reproducible builds; pinning base image digests
0.0.0.0 binding inside containers (Week 6 again)

resources.text: Liz Rice's talk Containers From Scratch (YouTube) — build a container in ~100 lines of Go
Docker docs: Get started and Dockerfile best practices
Julia Evans' How Containers Work zine
Docker Deep Dive (Nigel Poulton)

checklist.text: Watch Containers From Scratch. Use unshare and nsenter in a terminal to make a namespace by hand.
Docker get-started. Containerize your API; inspect image layers with docker history.
Multi-stage build; shrink the image; run as a non-root user; fix SIGTERM handling with --init. Scan with Trivy.

Follow Liz Rice's talk and type her mini container runtime along with her (it's in Go; she explains each line, and you don't need to know Go). Stretch: extend it yourself. Then Docker Compose your whole stack: Next.js + API + Postgres + Redis + NGINX.

main.doneWhen: you can explain why a container is not a VM, show the namespaces of a running container from the host, and explain why Dockerfile line order changes build time.

main.title: Kubernetes I — the model and core objects
main.why: Kubernetes is a control loop that keeps reality matching a YAML file. Learn that idea and the objects stop being a vocabulary list.

mustKnow.t: The problem: running many containers on many machines, restarting failures, scaling, rolling out new versions
Declarative desired state + reconciliation loops (controllers compare desired vs actual and act)
Architecture
c: Control plane: API server, etcd (the cluster's database), scheduler, controller manager
Nodes: kubelet, container runtime (containerd), kube-proxy

mustKnow.t: Core objects
c: Pod (one or more containers sharing network and storage), pod lifecycle
ReplicaSet, Deployment (rolling updates, rollbacks), StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob
Service: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer; how Services get stable IPs and DNS names; Endpoints/EndpointSlices
ConfigMap and Secret (and that Secrets are only base64 by default)

mainGroups.title: Learn to program
mainGroups.goal: go from never having programmed to writing, compiling and debugging small C programs, so every build in Phase 2 is within reach.
mainGroups.milestone: you've solved CS50x Problem Sets 1 and 2 with every check green.

mainGroups.title: Computers, OS, Linux, Git, Networks
mainGroups.goal: when you type a URL and press Enter, you can explain every step down to processes and packets. Everything after this phase sits on top of it.
mainGroups.milestone: write the first half of What happens when I type a URL, from keypress to the HTML bytes arriving. Optional buffer week before Phase 3.

mainGroups.title: The Browser, HTML, CSS, JavaScript
mainGroups.goal: you know what the browser does with every byte the server sends, and you know JavaScript as a language and as a runtime, not just syntax. No frameworks in this phase.
mainGroups.milestone: add the browser half to What happens when I type a URL: parsing, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite, script execution. Optional buffer week.

mainGroups.title: Backend and Databases
mainGroups.goal: you can build a production-shaped API and explain what happens inside Node and inside the database for every request. The main book for this phase is Designing Data- Intensive Applications (DDIA) by Martin Kleppmann and Chris Riccomini; get the 2nd edition (2026), which every chapter number in this plan refers to.
mainGroups.milestone: a Node + Postgres + Redis API with auth, validation, pagination, rate limiting, background jobs, tests and logging, in your foundations repo. Add the server half to What happens when I type a URL. Optional buffer week.

mainGroups.title: Engineering craft
mainGroups.goal: write code other people can change, find your way and fix bugs in codebases you didn't write, structure an application so its rules stay separate from its frameworks, and work the way teams work.
mainGroups.milestone: your Phase 4 API is refactored, layered and partly ported to NestJS, and you have an open or merged PR in a real open-source project.

mainGroups.title: Python and AI engineering
mainGroups.goal: pick up Python as a working second language, use AI coding tools without trusting them blindly, and build LLM features that are tested, safe and affordable.
mainGroups.milestone: your API has an AI feature with retrieval, citations, guardrails and an eval suite running in CI.

mainGroups.title: Build Tools, React, Next.js Internals
mainGroups.goal: Next.js stops being magic. You can explain how a component becomes HTML on a server, becomes JS chunks in a browser, and becomes interactive, and why each step exists.
mainGroups.milestone: mini bundler + mini React + a Next.js app with a How this page loads write-up. Optional buffer week.

mainGroups.title: Infrastructure and Deployment
mainGroups.goal: you can draw and explain the path of a real production request: user → DNS → CDN → WAF → load balancer → API gateway → Kubernetes Ingress → Service → Pod → your Node process → database.
mainGroups.milestone: draw your full production architecture from memory, every box labeled and justified. Add the infrastructure section to What happens when I type a URL. Optional buffer week.

mainGroups.title: System Design, Capstone and Career
mainGroups.goal: you can design a system for a given scale, justify every choice, and name the tradeoffs. Every building block is now something you've built a toy version of.
mainGroups.milestone: your capstone was designed, reviewed, built, deployed to the cloud and operated through a game day, and your portfolio shows it.

javaGroups.title: Programming in Java, OOP and Paradigms
javaGroups.goal: go from never having written Java to writing clean, object-oriented and functional Java, knowing how the JVM runs it, and analyzing an algorithm's cost. dev.java (Oracle's official tutorials for current Java) is your daily guide, and Exercism's Java exercises check themselves in IntelliJ, so you always know if you've got it.
javaGroups.milestone: you can write well-structured Java with classes, interfaces, generics, collections and streams, explain the four pillars of OOP and the main paradigms, and analyze complexity. Optional buffer week before Part C.

javaGroups.title: Object-Oriented Design
javaGroups.goal: use the OOP of Part A to design real programs: the everyday design patterns, then low-level design case studies like the ones in interviews.
javaGroups.milestone: you can design a parking lot, a booking system and an expense splitter in an hour each, with tests for the tricky rules.

javaGroups.title: Core Data Structures and Algorithms
javaGroups.goal: implement every core data structure from scratch, understand how Java's own versions work inside, and solve easy and medium problems by recognizing patterns. Each week: Tuesday learn, Thursday build it yourself, Sunday solve problems.
javaGroups.milestone: in under 20 minutes each and from a blank file, you can implement a dynamic array, hash map, linked list, stack, queue, BST and heap, and you've solved ~90 problems by pattern. Optional buffer week before Part E.

javaGroups.title: Java Backend with Spring Boot
javaGroups.goal: build production-shaped Java services with Spring Boot: dependency injection, REST, JPA, transactions, security, Kafka and observability.
javaGroups.milestone: two Spring Boot services that authenticate, persist with JPA, talk through Kafka and run from container images.

javaGroups.title: Advanced Algorithms and Practice
